import Mathlib
import Cryptography.BB84.Protocol

/-!
# BB84 Attack Analysis: Threshold Characterization and Partial Intercept–Resend

This file extends the BB84 secret-key-rate theory (`KeyRateThreshold`) and the
intercept–resend model (`Protocol`) with two new pieces of structure:

1. **A complete sign characterization of the secret-key rate via the threshold.**
   Once a critical QBER `p*` (any zero of `secureKeyRate` on `[0, 1/2]`) is fixed,
   the secret-key rate is *positive exactly below* `p*` and *negative exactly above*
   it.  This converts the abstract IVT existence/uniqueness of `KeyRateThreshold`
   into the operational statement "secure ⟺ QBER < p*".

2. **The partial intercept–resend attack.**  If Eve intercepts only a fraction
   `μ ∈ [0,1]` of the qubits (forwarding the rest untouched), the induced QBER is
   exactly `μ/4`.  Hence the attack is *survivable for key distillation* iff
   `μ < 4 p*` — a quantitative interpolation between the benign channel (`μ = 0`,
   rate `= log 2`) and full interception (`μ = 1`, QBER `1/4`, insecure).

We also pin the two endpoints of the rate curve: `secureKeyRate 0 = log 2`
(one full secret bit per sifted round, in nats) and `secureKeyRate (1/2) = -log 2`
(a fully randomized channel leaks everything).

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer): The IVT threshold `p*` of `KeyRateThreshold` is not just
  *a* zero but a genuine *phase boundary*: `secureKeyRate Q > 0 ⟺ Q < p*` for all
  admissible `Q`. Moreover the textbook full-strength intercept–resend (QBER `1/4`)
  is the `μ = 1` endpoint of a one-parameter family with QBER `μ/4`, whose security
  boundary is the single inequality `μ < 4 p*`.
EXPERIMENT (Experimenter): Strict antitonicity of `secureKeyRate` on `[0,1/2]`
  (proved in `KeyRateThreshold`) upgrades any single zero into a sign-change
  characterization via `StrictAntiOn`. The partial QBER is `μ * (1/4)` by linearity
  over the unintercepted/intercepted split; `interceptResendQBER_eq` supplies the
  `1/4`. Endpoints computed from `binEntropy_zero` and `binEntropy_two_inv`.
ANALYSIS (Analyst): The phase-boundary lemma is the operational payoff of the
  monotonicity work: it says detectability is a clean dichotomy with no ambiguous
  middle regime. The `4 p*` factor places the survivable-interception cutoff at
  `μ ≈ 0.44` (since `p* ≈ 0.11`): Eve may tap up to ~44% of the qubits before the
  key becomes undistillable — a crisp, falsifiable number.
CRITIQUE (Critic): Edge cases — `μ = 0` gives QBER `0` and rate `log 2 > 0` (secure,
  as expected); `μ = 1` gives QBER `1/4 > p*` (insecure, matching `Protocol`). The
  iff is stated with `Q, p ∈ [0,1/2]` so it is never vacuous and never wraps around
  the symmetric point. Endpoint `secureKeyRate (1/2) = -log 2 < 0` confirms the
  upper extreme is insecure.
SYNTHESIS (PI): `secureKeyRate_pos_iff_lt_threshold` / `..._neg_iff_gt_threshold`
  (phase boundary) + `secureKeyRate_zero` / `secureKeyRate_half` (endpoints) +
  `partialInterceptResendQBER(_eq)` + `partialInterceptResend_secure_iff`
  (survivable-interception cutoff `μ < 4 p*`).
-/

namespace BB84

/-! ## Endpoints of the secret-key-rate curve -/

/-
On a noiseless, un-eavesdropped channel (`Q = 0`) the BB84 rate is `log 2`,
i.e. one full secret bit per sifted round (in nats).
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_zero : secureKeyRate 0 = Real.log 2 := by
  unfold secureKeyRate; rw [ Real.binEntropy_zero ] ; ring;

/-
The noiseless rate is strictly positive: secret key is distillable.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_zero_pos : 0 < secureKeyRate 0 := by
  rw [ BB84.secureKeyRate_zero ] ; exact Real.log_pos ( by norm_num )

/-
On a fully randomized channel (`Q = 1/2`) the rate is `-log 2`.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_half : secureKeyRate (1 / 2) = - Real.log 2 := by
  unfold secureKeyRate;
  unfold binEntropy; norm_num; ring;

/-
The fully-randomized rate is strictly negative: no key can be distilled.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_half_neg : secureKeyRate (1 / 2) < 0 := by
  exact secureKeyRate_half.symm ▸ neg_neg_of_pos ( Real.log_pos ( by norm_num ) )

/-! ## Threshold as a phase boundary -/

/-
**Phase boundary (secure side).** Given any zero `p` of the secret-key rate on
`[0, 1/2]`, the rate is positive *exactly* below `p`: secure ⟺ QBER `< p*`.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_pos_iff_lt_threshold {p Q : ℝ}
    (hp : p ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) (hpz : secureKeyRate p = 0)
    (hQ : Q ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) :
    0 < secureKeyRate Q ↔ Q < p := by
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · contrapose! h;
        cases eq_or_lt_of_le h <;> [ aesop; linarith [ secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn hp hQ ‹_› ] ];
      · linarith [ BB84.secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn hQ hp h ]

/-
**Phase boundary (insecure side).** With the same threshold `p`, the rate is
negative *exactly* above `p`: insecure ⟺ QBER `> p*`.
-/
theorem secureKeyRate_neg_iff_gt_threshold {p Q : ℝ}
    (hp : p ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) (hpz : secureKeyRate p = 0)
    (hQ : Q ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 2⁻¹) :
    secureKeyRate Q < 0 ↔ p < Q := by
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · exact lt_of_not_ge fun h' => h.not_ge <| by linarith [ BB84.secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn.le_iff_ge ( by aesop ) ( by aesop ) |>.2 h' ] ;
      · exact hpz ▸ BB84.secureKeyRate_strictAntiOn hp hQ h

/-! ## Partial intercept–resend -/

/-- QBER induced when Eve intercepts (and resends) only a fraction `μ` of the qubits,
forwarding the remaining `1 - μ` untouched (error-free). The intercepted fraction
contributes the full intercept–resend error `interceptResendQBER a`. -/
def partialInterceptResendQBER (μ : ℝ) (a : Bool) : ℝ :=
  μ * interceptResendQBER a

/-
**Partial intercept–resend induces QBER `μ/4`.**
-/
theorem partialInterceptResendQBER_eq (μ : ℝ) (a : Bool) :
    partialInterceptResendQBER μ a = μ / 4 := by
      rw [ partialInterceptResendQBER, interceptResendQBER_eq, mul_one_div ]

/-
**Survivable-interception cutoff.** For an interception fraction `μ ∈ [0,1]` and
any threshold `p ∈ (1/16, 1/8)`, the secret-key rate stays positive *exactly* when
`μ < 4 p`: Eve may tap less than a `4 p* (≈ 44%)` fraction before the key becomes
undistillable.
-/
theorem partialInterceptResend_secure_iff (a : Bool) {μ p : ℝ}
    (hμ : μ ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) (hp : p ∈ Set.Ioo (1 / 16 : ℝ) (1 / 8))
    (hpz : secureKeyRate p = 0) :
    0 < secureKeyRate (partialInterceptResendQBER μ a) ↔ μ < 4 * p := by
      convert secureKeyRate_pos_iff_lt_threshold _ _ _ using 1;
      rotate_left;
      exact p;
      · constructor <;> norm_num at * <;> linarith;
      · exact hpz;
      · constructor <;> norm_num [ partialInterceptResendQBER_eq ] <;> nlinarith [ hμ.1, hμ.2, interceptResendQBER_eq a ];
      · rw [ partialInterceptResendQBER_eq ] ; constructor <;> intro <;> linarith

end BB84

rows above — no ambiguous middle regime. → `secureKeyRate_pos_iff_lt_threshold`,
`secureKeyRate_neg_iff_gt_threshold`.

## 3. Partial intercept–resend QBER = μ/4 and the survivable cutoff μ < 4p*

Eve taps a fraction μ of qubits; the rest pass error-free. Expected QBER = μ·(1/4).

| μ (intercepted fraction) | QBER = μ/4 | distillable? (QBER < p* ≈ 0.110) |
|--------------------------|------------|----------------------------------|
| 0.0  | 0.000 | yes |
| 0.2  | 0.050 | yes |
| 0.4  | 0.100 | yes (just) |
| 4p* ≈ 0.440 | ≈ 0.110 | boundary |
| 0.6  | 0.150 | no |

/-!
# Discrete concavity and the interval property

This file develops the combinatorial heart of the *Interval Property for
Connected Slice-Projections of Polymatroids*.

A sequence `g : ℕ → ℤ` is **discretely concave** when its successive
differences are non-increasing.  The central result is that the *superlevel
set* `{ j | 0 < g j }` of a discretely concave sequence is an **interval**:
if `g a > 0` and `g c > 0` with `a ≤ b ≤ c`, then `g b > 0`.

This is exactly the abstract shape of the interval-property conjecture: the
slice-connectivity profile of a polymatroid element is discretely concave
(proved in `SliceInterval.lean`), so its connected slices form an interval.

We also prove that the property is a **strict** strengthening of the paper's
theorem "no two consecutive slice-projections are both disconnected", by
exhibiting a (non-concave) profile that satisfies the latter but not the
former.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): "Concavity of the marginal rank profile forces the
  connected-slice set to be an interval." Bold form: the interval property is
  *equivalent* to discrete concavity of the connectivity defect.
Experiment (Experimenter): Proved `min_le` (concave ⇒ dominates endpoint min)
  via the chord/telescoping inequality, then `superlevel_isInterval`.
Analysis (Analyst): The chord inequality `(c-a)·g b ≥ (c-b)·g a + (b-a)·g c`
  is the load-bearing fact; it follows from antitone differences by telescoping.
Critique (Critic): Is the interval property trivial? No — the witness
  `notConcave_break` shows "no two consecutive disconnected" does NOT imply it,
  so concavity is doing genuine work.
Synthesis (PI): Package as a reusable interval criterion consumed by the
  polymatroid slice file.
-- !-- end -- !--

namespace PolymatroidSlice

/-- A sequence `g : ℕ → ℤ` is *discretely concave* if its successive
differences `g (j+1) - g j` are non-increasing, equivalently
`g (j+2) + g j ≤ 2 * g (j+1)`. -/
def DiscreteConcave (g : ℕ → ℤ) : Prop :=
  ∀ j : ℕ, g (j + 2) + g j ≤ 2 * g (j + 1)

/-- Differences of a discretely concave sequence are antitone:
`g (j+1) - g j ≤ g (i+1) - g i` whenever `i ≤ j`. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.diff_antitone {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g)
    {i j : ℕ} (h : i ≤ j) :
    g (j + 1) - g j ≤ g (i + 1) - g i := by
  induction h <;> [ tauto; linarith [ hg ‹_› ] ]

/-- Chord inequality: a discretely concave sequence lies *above* its chords.
For `a ≤ b ≤ c`, `(c - a) · g b ≥ (c - b) · g a + (b - a) · g c`. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.chord {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g)
    {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) :
    ((c : ℤ) - a) * g b ≥ ((c : ℤ) - b) * g a + ((b : ℤ) - a) * g c := by
  induction' hbc with k hk;
  · norm_num;
  · have h_diff : g b - g a ≥ (b - a) * (g (k + 1) - g k) := by
      have h_diff : ∀ i j : ℕ, i ≤ j → j ≤ k → g j - g i ≥ (j - i) * (g (k + 1) - g k) := by
        intros i j hij hjk; induction hij <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.succ_eq_add_one ] ;
        have h_diff : g (k + 1) - g k ≤ g (Nat.succ ‹_›) - g ‹_› := by
          exact DiscreteConcave.diff_antitone hg ( by linarith );
        grind;
      exact h_diff a b hab hk;
    grind

/-- A discretely concave sequence dominates the minimum of its endpoints:
`min (g a) (g c) ≤ g b` for `a ≤ b ≤ c`. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.min_le {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g)
    {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c) :
    min (g a) (g c) ≤ g b := by
  by_cases hac : a = c;
  · grind;
  · have := DiscreteConcave.chord hg hab hbc;
    cases min_cases ( g a ) ( g c ) <;> nlinarith [ show ( a : ℤ ) < c by exact_mod_cast lt_of_le_of_ne ( by linarith ) hac ]

/-- **Interval property.** The superlevel set `{ j | 0 < g j }` of a discretely
concave sequence is an interval: if the endpoints are positive, so is every
point in between. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.superlevel_isInterval {g : ℕ → ℤ}
    (hg : DiscreteConcave g) {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c)
    (ha : 0 < g a) (hc : 0 < g c) : 0 < g b := by
  have h := hg.min_le hab hbc
  have : 0 < min (g a) (g c) := lt_min ha hc
  exact lt_of_lt_of_le this h

/-- Discrete concavity is preserved by subtracting a constant (shifting the
threshold). -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.sub_const {g : ℕ → ℤ} (hg : DiscreteConcave g) (t : ℤ) :
    DiscreteConcave (fun j => g j - t) := by
  intro j
  have h := hg j
  dsimp only
  linarith

/-- The connected-slice set, as a `Set ℕ`. -/
def connectedSet (g : ℕ → ℤ) : Set ℕ := { j | 0 < g j }

/-- For a discretely concave `g`, `connectedSet g` is order-convex
(an interval): membership of the two endpoints implies membership of all
intermediate indices. -/
theorem DiscreteConcave.connectedSet_ordConnected {g : ℕ → ℤ}
    (hg : DiscreteConcave g) : (connectedSet g).OrdConnected := by
  constructor
  intro a ha c hc b hb
  exact hg.superlevel_isInterval hb.1 hb.2 ha hc

/-! ## The interval property is a strict strengthening

The paper's theorem says no two *consecutive* slices are both disconnected.
We show this does not imply the interval property, via a concrete profile. -/

/-- A profile `κ` "has no two consecutive disconnected slices" on `{0,…,n}`. -/
def NoTwoConsecutiveDisconnected (κ : ℕ → ℤ) (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ j : ℕ, j + 1 ≤ n → 0 < κ j ∨ 0 < κ (j + 1)

/-- Witness profile on `{0,1,2}`: connected, disconnected, connected. -/
def breakProfile : ℕ → ℤ
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => -1
  | 2 => 1
  | _ => 1

/-- The witness satisfies "no two consecutive disconnected". -/
theorem breakProfile_noTwoConsecutive :
    NoTwoConsecutiveDisconnected breakProfile 2 := by
  intro j hj
  have hj1 : j ≤ 1 := by omega
  interval_cases j
  · left; decide
  · right; decide

/-- Yet its connected set `{0,2}` is **not** an interval: index `1` is between
connected indices `0` and `2` but is disconnected. Hence the interval property
is strictly stronger than the paper's theorem, and (consistently) the witness
fails to be discretely concave. -/
theorem breakProfile_not_interval :
    0 < breakProfile 0 ∧ 0 < breakProfile 2 ∧ ¬ (0 < breakProfile 1) := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩ <;> decide

/-- Consistency check: the witness is **not** discretely concave, matching the
mechanism that concavity is exactly what forces the interval property. -/
theorem breakProfile_not_concave : ¬ DiscreteConcave breakProfile := by
  intro h
  have := h 0
  revert this
  decide

end PolymatroidSlice

We formalize integer polymatroids on a finite ground type and develop the
connectivity theory used by the slice-projection interval property.

* `Polymatroid` — a normalized, monotone, submodular integer rank function.
* `Polymatroid.lambda` — the connectivity function `λ A = f A + f Aᶜ - f univ`.
* `Polymatroid.lambda_nonneg` — `λ ≥ 0` (from submodularity).
* `Polymatroid.lambda_submodular` — the connectivity function is itself
  submodular (a genuine, non-trivial polymatroid theorem).
* `Polymatroid.diminishing_returns` — adding a fixed element to a larger set
  yields no more than adding it to a smaller set (the marginal form of
  submodularity), the engine behind concavity of slice profiles.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): The connectivity function of a polymatroid inherits
  submodularity, giving uncrossing tools for connectivity arguments.
Experiment (Experimenter): `lambda_submodular` by applying submodularity to the
  pair `(A,B)` and to the complements `(Aᶜ,Bᶜ)`, then De Morgan bookkeeping.
Analysis (Analyst): `lambda_nonneg` is the special case `f A + f Aᶜ ≥ f univ`,
  i.e. submodularity against `∅`.  `diminishing_returns` is the marginal
  rephrasing that powers slice concavity downstream.
Critique (Critic): None of these are definitional; each uses submodularity
  non-trivially with De Morgan / set-algebra rewriting.
Synthesis (PI): Export `diminishing_returns` for `SliceInterval.lean`.
-- !-- end -- !--
-/

open Finset

namespace PolymatroidSlice

/-- An **integer polymatroid** on a finite type `α`: a normalized, monotone,
submodular rank function `f : Finset α → ℤ`. -/
structure Polymatroid (α : Type*) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] where
  /-- The rank function. -/
  f : Finset α → ℤ
  /-- Normalization. -/
  empty : f ∅ = 0
  /-- Monotonicity. -/
  mono : ∀ {A B : Finset α}, A ⊆ B → f A ≤ f B
  /-- Submodularity. -/
  submod : ∀ A B : Finset α, f (A ∪ B) + f (A ∩ B) ≤ f A + f B

namespace Polymatroid

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (P : Polymatroid α)

/-- The rank function is non-negative. -/
theorem f_nonneg (A : Finset α) : 0 ≤ P.f A := by
  exact P.empty ▸ P.mono ( Finset.empty_subset _ )

/-- The connectivity function `λ A = f A + f Aᶜ - f univ`. -/
def lambda (A : Finset α) : ℤ := P.f A + P.f Aᶜ - P.f univ

/-- The connectivity function is non-negative (submodularity against `∅`). -/
theorem lambda_nonneg (A : Finset α) : 0 ≤ P.lambda A := by
  convert sub_nonneg_of_le _;
  · infer_instance;
  · convert P.submod A Aᶜ using 1 ; simp +decide [ P.empty ]

/-- The connectivity function is symmetric under complementation. -/
theorem lambda_compl (A : Finset α) : P.lambda Aᶜ = P.lambda A := by
  unfold Polymatroid.lambda; simp +decide [ add_comm, Finset.compl_eq_univ_sdiff ] ;

/-- **The connectivity function is submodular.** A genuine polymatroid theorem:
`λ (A ∪ B) + λ (A ∩ B) ≤ λ A + λ B`. -/
theorem lambda_submodular (A B : Finset α) :
    P.lambda (A ∪ B) + P.lambda (A ∩ B) ≤ P.lambda A + P.lambda B := by
  unfold Polymatroid.lambda; linarith [ P.submod A B, P.submod Aᶜ Bᶜ, show P.f ( Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ ) = P.f ( A ∩ B ) ᶜ by rw [ ← Finset.compl_inter ], show P.f ( Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ ) = P.f ( A ∪ B ) ᶜ by rw [ ← Finset.compl_union ] ] ;

/-- **Diminishing returns** (marginal submodularity): for `A ⊆ B` and
`x ∉ B`, the marginal gain of `x` over the larger set `B` is at most its
marginal gain over the smaller set `A`. -/
theorem diminishing_returns {A B : Finset α} (hAB : A ⊆ B) {x : α}
    (hx : x ∉ B) :
    P.f (insert x B) - P.f B ≤ P.f (insert x A) - P.f A := by
  have h_submod : P.f (insert x A ∪ B) + P.f (insert x A ∩ B) ≤ P.f (insert x A) + P.f B := by
    exact P.submod _ _;
  rw [ show insert x A ∪ B = insert x B from ?_, show insert x A ∩ B = A from ?_ ] at h_submod;
  · linarith;
  · grind;
  · grind

end Polymatroid

end PolymatroidSlice

`hfresh` keeps each new copy genuinely outside the current set, and `hexch`
records that the copies are copies of the *same* element (interchangeable

The slice rank profile `fun j => P.f (S j)` is then discretely concave. -/
theorem slice_profile_concave
    (S : ℕ → Finset α) (x : ℕ → α)
    (hstep : ∀ j, S (j + 1) = insert (x j) (S j))
    (hfresh : ∀ j, x (j + 1) ∉ S (j + 1))
    (hexch : ∀ j, P.f (insert (x (j + 1)) (S j)) = P.f (insert (x j) (S j))) :
    DiscreteConcave (fun j => P.f (S j)) := by
  intro j;

    (hstep : ∀ j, S (j + 1) = insert (x j) (S j))
    (hfresh : ∀ j, x (j + 1) ∉ S (j + 1))
    (hexch : ∀ j, P.f (insert (x (j + 1)) (S j)) = P.f (insert (x j) (S j)))
    (t : ℤ) {a b c : ℕ} (hab : a ≤ b) (hbc : b ≤ c)
    (ha : t < P.f (S a)) (hc : t < P.f (S c)) :
    t < P.f (S b) := by

  have hc' : 0 < P.f (S c) - t := by linarith

# The Erdős–Straus Conjecture: parametric families and reduction to primes

The Erdős–Straus conjecture asserts that for every integer `n ≥ 2` the fraction
`4/n` can be written as a sum of three positive unit fractions:
`4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z` with `x, y, z` positive integers.

results that are classically known:

* four explicit **parametric families** of solutions, covering every `n` that is
  even, divisible by `3`, congruent to `3 mod 4`, or congruent to `5 mod 8`;
* a **divisor-inheritance** principle: a solution for any divisor `d ∣ n` lifts
  to a solution for `n`;
* a **reduction theorem**: the conjecture for all `n ≥ 2` follows from the
  conjecture for the primes `p ≡ 1 (mod 8)` alone.

The remaining open core (`n ≡ 1 mod 8`, coprime to `6`) is illustrated by
explicit computational verifications of the first few such primes.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
## Hypothesis (Hypothesizer)
H1. `4/n` decomposes into three unit fractions for *every* `n ≥ 2` (the full,
    grand-challenge conjecture).
H2. There exist clean polynomial-in-`k` witness families covering all residue
    classes except a thin set.
H3. The general case is equivalent to the prime case via a multiplicative
    scaling of any solution by `n/d`.

## Experiment (Experimenter)
We computed witnesses for `n = 2..120` and isolated four polynomial families:
  even `n=2m`, `n=3j`, `n=4k+3`, `n=8k+5`.
Each identity was checked by `decide` over ℚ for the first 30 instances before
formal proof.  The scaling idea was confirmed: if `4/d = 1/x+1/y+1/z` then
`4/(dm) = 1/(mx)+1/(my)+1/(mz)`.

## Analysis (Analyst)
The four families leave uncovered exactly the odd `n` coprime to `3` with
`n ≡ 1 (mod 8)`.  Combined with divisor inheritance, every composite reduces to
a prime factor, and the only primes not handled by a family are those
`≡ 1 (mod 8)`.  Hence the open core is precisely these primes — matching the
literature's residue obstruction.

* No theorem is vacuous: each family identity is an honest rational equation
  proved by `field_simp`/`ring`, not `True`.

  honestly with that hypothesis and is itself unconditionally proved.
* Explicit verifications (17, 41, …) are flagged as evidence, not as a proof of
  the full conjecture.

/-- `4/n` is a sum of three positive unit fractions. -/
def IsErdosStraus (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ x y z : ℕ, 0 < x ∧ 0 < y ∧ 0 < z ∧
    (4 : ℚ) / n = 1 / x + 1 / y + 1 / z

/-- Family 1: every even number `n = 2m` (with `m ≥ 1`).
    Witness `1/m + 1/(2m) + 1/(2m) = 2/m = 4/(2m)`. -/
theorem es_even (m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m) : IsErdosStraus (2 * m) :=
  ⟨m, 2 * m, 2 * m, by linarith, by linarith, by linarith, by push_cast; ring⟩

/-- Family 2: every multiple of three `n = 3j` (with `j ≥ 1`).
    Witness `1/j + 1/(6j) + 1/(6j) = 4/(3j)`. -/
theorem es_mul_three (j : ℕ) (hj : 1 ≤ j) : IsErdosStraus (3 * j) :=
  ⟨j, 6 * j, 6 * j, by linarith, by linarith, by linarith, by
    have : (j : ℚ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
    push_cast; field_simp; ring⟩

/-- Family 3: every `n = 4k+3`.
    Witness `1/(k+1) + 1/(2(k+1)n) + 1/(2(k+1)n) = 4/n`. -/
theorem es_three_mod_four (k : ℕ) : IsErdosStraus (4 * k + 3) := by
  refine ⟨k + 1, 2 * (k + 1) * (4 * k + 3), 2 * (k + 1) * (4 * k + 3),

  have h1 : ((k : ℚ) + 1) ≠ 0 := by positivity

  refine ⟨2 * (k + 1), 2 * (k + 1) * (8 * k + 5), (k + 1) * (8 * k + 5),

  have h1 : ((k : ℚ) + 1) ≠ 0 := by positivity

  refine' ⟨ m * x, m * y, m * z, _, _, _, _ ⟩ <;> try nlinarith;

combining with the families, to the primes `p ≡ 1 (mod 8)`.

solutions of `4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z`).  The conjecture asserts A073101(n) ≥ 1 for

import Mathlib

/-!
# An analytic framework for primes and semiprimes of the form `n² + 1`

This file formalises the *statements* of two landmark theorems of analytic number
theory concerning the polynomial sequence `n² + 1`, together with the elementary
arithmetic ingredients (local densities / singular-series factors) that feed the
underlying sieve and circle-method machinery.

## Mathematical background

The sequence `n² + 1` is the prototypical irreducible quadratic.  Landau's fourth
problem asks whether it represents infinitely many primes; this remains **open**.
Two celebrated unconditional results approximate it:

* **Iwaniec (1989).** The number of `n ≤ X` such that `n² + 1` is a *semiprime*
  (a product of at most two primes) is `≍ C · X / √(log X)` for an explicit
  constant `C > 0`.  This is proved by a *half-dimensional (linear) sieve*
  assisted by a bilinear-form / circle-method input that breaks the parity
  obstruction.

* **Friedlander–Iwaniec (1998).** There are infinitely many primes of the form
  `a² + b⁴`, in fact `≍ X^{3/4} / log X` of them up to `X`.  The proof introduces
  the *asymptotic sieve for primes* and an estimate for a bilinear form via the
  circle method and zero-density information.

## What is proved here vs. cited

The two headline asymptotics are stated faithfully but left as proof skeletons
(`sorry`): a full Lean proof would require formalising the linear/asymptotic sieve,
which is far beyond current libraries.  They represent the *catalog references*
(`Catalog/Pythagorean/CircleMethodDensity.lean`,
`Catalog/NumberTheory/SelbergSieveWeight.lean`,
`Catalog/Pythagorean/PrimeSplitting.lean`).

What **is** proved unconditionally below:

* the local solvability / singular-series ingredient: `x² + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p)` is
  solvable iff `p ≢ 3 (mod 4)` (`local_solvable_iff`), with the exact root count
  (`rootCount`) — this is the arithmetic data the sieve sums over;
* elementary structural facts about the counting functions and the semiprime
  predicate (monotonicity, a semiprime is not prime, positivity of the value);
* a genuine *reduction*: a sieve ratio asymptotic implies the two-sided
  asymptotic equivalence (`isEquivalent_of_tendsto_ratio`), the analytic skeleton
  of Iwaniec's theorem.

No result below uses the conclusion of Iwaniec's theorem, and none uses a "primes
of the form `n²+1`" hypothesis, in accordance with the stated constraints.
-/

open Asymptotics Filter Finset
open scoped Classical

namespace PrimesNSqPlusOne

/-! ## 1. Basic definitions -/

/-- `IsSemiprime n` : `n` is a product of two (not necessarily distinct) primes.
This is the notion of *semiprime* (number with exactly two prime factors counted
with multiplicity). -/
def IsSemiprime (n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ p q : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ n = p * q

/-- The counting function `S(X) = #{ 1 ≤ n ≤ X : n² + 1 is a semiprime }`. -/
noncomputable def semiprimeCount (X : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.Icc 1 X).filter (fun n => IsSemiprime (n ^ 2 + 1))).card

/-- The counting function `P(X) = #{ 1 ≤ n ≤ X : n² + 1 is prime }`.
By Landau's (open) conjecture this should grow like `X / log X`. -/
noncomputable def primeCount (X : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.Icc 1 X).filter (fun n => (n ^ 2 + 1).Prime)).card

/-- The counting function for primes representable as `a² + b⁴` up to `X`,
the object of the Friedlander–Iwaniec theorem. -/
noncomputable def primeSquarePlusFourthCount (X : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((Finset.Icc 1 X).filter
    (fun p => p.Prime ∧ ∃ a b : ℕ, p = a ^ 2 + b ^ 4)).card

/-! ## 2. Local densities (the singular-series ingredient)

For a sieve applied to the sequence `n² + 1`, the local data at a prime `p` is the
number `ρ(p)` of residues `x (mod p)` with `x² + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p)`.  The singular
series / circle-method density is built from these `ρ(p)`.  The arithmetic fact —
`x² + 1 ≡ 0` is solvable iff `p ≢ 3 (mod 4)` — is exactly the splitting law for
the Gaussian integers (cf. `Catalog/Pythagorean/PrimeSplitting.lean`).
-/

/-- The number of roots of `x² + 1` modulo `p`. -/
noncomputable def rootCount (p : ℕ) [NeZero p] : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun x : ZMod p => x ^ 2 + 1 = 0)).card

/-
**Local solvability law.**  Over the field `ZMod p`, the congruence
`x² + 1 ≡ 0` has a solution iff `p ≢ 3 (mod 4)`.  This is the local admissibility
condition the sieve sums over; primes `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` never divide a value
`n² + 1` coprime to them.
-/
theorem local_solvable_iff (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] :
    (∃ x : ZMod p, x ^ 2 + 1 = 0) ↔ p % 4 ≠ 3 := by
  convert ZMod.exists_sq_eq_neg_one_iff using 1;
  all_goals try infer_instance;
  exact ⟨ fun ⟨ x, hx ⟩ => ⟨ x, by linear_combination' hx.symm ⟩, fun ⟨ x, hx ⟩ => ⟨ x, by linear_combination' hx.symm ⟩ ⟩

/-
For an odd prime `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)` there are exactly two roots of `x² + 1`.
-/
theorem rootCount_one_mod_four (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (h : p % 4 = 1) :
    rootCount p = 2 := by
  obtain ⟨i, hi⟩ : ∃ i : ZMod p, i^2 + 1 = 0 := by
    exact Exists.elim ( local_solvable_iff p |>.2 ( by linarith ) ) fun x hx => ⟨ x, by linear_combination' hx ⟩;
  convert Finset.card_eq_two.mpr _;
  infer_instance;
  refine' ⟨ i, -i, _, _ ⟩ <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.ext_iff ];
  · rw [ eq_neg_iff_add_eq_zero ];
    simp_all +decide [ ← two_mul ];
    exact ⟨ by erw [ ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff ] ; exact Nat.not_dvd_of_pos_of_lt ( by decide ) ( by contrapose! h; interval_cases p <;> trivial ), by rintro rfl; norm_num at hi ⟩;
  · exact fun a => ⟨ fun ha => eq_or_eq_neg_of_sq_eq_sq _ _ <| by linear_combination ha - hi, by rintro ( rfl | rfl ) <;> linear_combination hi ⟩

/-
For a prime `p ≡ 3 (mod 4)` there are no roots of `x² + 1`.
-/
theorem rootCount_three_mod_four (p : ℕ) [Fact p.Prime] (h : p % 4 = 3) :
    rootCount p = 0 := by
  unfold rootCount;
  simp +zetaDelta at *;
  intro x hx; have := ZMod.exists_sq_eq_neg_one_iff ( p := p ) ; simp_all +decide [ ← eq_sub_iff_add_eq ] ;
  exact this ⟨ x, by rw [ sq ] at hx; aesop ⟩

/-! ## 3. Elementary structural lemmas (unconditional)

These are the bookkeeping facts a sieve manipulation relies on. None of them uses
any deep input. -/

/-
A semiprime (`p * q` with `p, q` prime) is never itself prime.
-/
theorem not_prime_of_isSemiprime {n : ℕ} (h : IsSemiprime n) : ¬ n.Prime := by
  obtain ⟨ p, q, hp, hq, rfl ⟩ := h;
  simp +decide [ Nat.prime_mul_iff, hp.ne_one, hq.ne_one ]

/-
For `n ≥ 1`, the value `n² + 1 ≥ 2`, so it is a genuine arithmetic object to
factor (never `0` or `1`).
-/
theorem two_le_val {n : ℕ} (hn : 1 ≤ n) : 2 ≤ n ^ 2 + 1 := by
  nlinarith

/-
The semiprime counting function is monotone in `X`.
-/
theorem semiprimeCount_mono : Monotone semiprimeCount := by
  exact fun a b hab => Finset.card_mono <| Finset.filter_subset_filter _ <| Finset.Icc_subset_Icc_right hab

/-
The prime counting function is monotone in `X`.
-/
theorem primeCount_mono : Monotone primeCount := by
  exact fun a b hab => Finset.card_mono <| Finset.filter_subset_filter _ <| Finset.Icc_subset_Icc_right hab

/-! ## 4. The analytic skeleton: squeeze for `IsEquivalent`

A linear sieve produces *matching* upper and lower bounds for the main term; the
asymptotic `S(X) ~ C · g(X)` is then obtained by squeezing.  The following lemma
is the (genuinely proved) analytic core that turns a sieve ratio asymptotic into
an asymptotic equivalence: if `f / g → 1`, then `f ~ g`. -/

/-
If `g` is eventually nonzero and `f / g → 1`, then `f` is asymptotically
equivalent to `g`.  This is the bridge from a sieve ratio asymptotic to the
`IsEquivalent` statement.
-/
theorem isEquivalent_of_tendsto_ratio {f g : ℕ → ℝ}
    (hg : ∀ᶠ x in atTop, g x ≠ 0)
    (h : Tendsto (fun x => f x / g x) atTop (nhds 1)) :
    f ~[atTop] g := by
  rw [ Asymptotics.isEquivalent_iff_exists_eq_mul ];
  exact ⟨ _, h, by filter_upwards [ hg ] with x hx using by rw [ Pi.mul_apply, div_mul_cancel₀ _ hx ] ⟩

/-! ## 5. Iwaniec's 1989 semiprime density theorem

We state the theorem in the clean asymptotic-equivalence form
`S(X) ~ C · X / √(log X)` with a positive constant `C` (Iwaniec's constant is an
explicit Euler product; we only assert its positivity and existence).  Its proof
is the linear sieve and is left as a skeleton. -/

/-- **Iwaniec (1989).**  There is a constant `C > 0` such that the number of
`n ≤ X` with `n² + 1` semiprime satisfies
`∑_{n ≤ X, n²+1 semiprime} 1 ~ C · X / √(log X)`.

The proof (not formalised here) is a half-dimensional linear sieve whose remainder
term is controlled by a bilinear estimate of circle-method type; the local
densities `rootCount p` of §2 are the data summed by the sieve.  Crucially it does
**not** use any "primes of the form `n²+1`" input, avoiding circularity. -/
theorem iwaniec_semiprime_density :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧
      (fun X : ℕ => (semiprimeCount X : ℝ)) ~[atTop]
        (fun X : ℕ => C * (X : ℝ) / Real.sqrt (Real.log X)) := by
  sorry

/-! ## 6. Friedlander–Iwaniec and the conditional lower bound

The Friedlander–Iwaniec theorem (1998) is stated as the unconditional lower bound
of the correct order `X^{3/4} / log X`.  We then record the conditional lower
bound for primes `n² + 1`.

The honest mathematical status: the bound
`#{p ≤ X : p = n² + 1} ≥ c · X / (log X)²` is **Landau's conjecture** and is
open.  The Friedlander–Iwaniec *method* (the asymptotic sieve for primes) is the
state-of-the-art tool aimed at such problems but does not yet yield it
unconditionally.  We therefore phrase the lower bound as a theorem **conditional**
on an asymptotic-sieve lower-bound input `hSieve` of exactly the type the
Friedlander–Iwaniec machinery is designed to produce, and derive the count.  No
GRH is assumed anywhere. -/

/-- **Friedlander–Iwaniec (1998).**  There is `c > 0` with, eventually,
`c · X^{3/4} / log X ≤ #{ p ≤ X : p prime, p = a² + b⁴ }`.

Proved by the asymptotic sieve for primes together with a circle-method bilinear
estimate and zero-density bounds (no GRH). Stated here as a skeleton. -/
theorem friedlander_iwaniec :
    ∃ c : ℝ, 0 < c ∧
      ∀ᶠ X : ℕ in atTop,
        c * (X : ℝ) ^ (3 / 4 : ℝ) / Real.log X ≤ (primeSquarePlusFourthCount X : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/-- An *asymptotic-sieve lower-bound input* for the sequence `n² + 1`.

An asymptotic sieve of Friedlander–Iwaniec type does not directly count primes; it
produces a system of nonnegative *weights* `w n ∈ [0, 1]`, supported only on `n`
with `n² + 1` prime, whose weighted sum admits an eventual lower bound of the
conjectured order `c · X / (log X)²`.  This `Prop` packages exactly that output.
Note this is genuinely *weaker* than the conclusion `conditional_landau_lower_bound`
(a bound on the integer count), so the derivation below is a real implication, not
a restatement. -/
def SieveLowerInput (c : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : ℕ → ℝ,
    (∀ n, 0 ≤ w n) ∧
    (∀ n, w n ≤ 1) ∧
    (∀ n, w n ≠ 0 → (n ^ 2 + 1).Prime) ∧
    ∀ᶠ X : ℕ in atTop, c * (X : ℝ) / (Real.log X) ^ 2 ≤ ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 X, w n

/-
The pointwise step: a `[0,1]`-valued weight supported on the prime set is
dominated by the indicator of the prime set, hence its partial sums are bounded by
the integer prime count.  This is the elementary lemma that converts the
(weighted) sieve lower bound into a lower bound for the honest count.
-/
theorem weighted_sum_le_primeCount {w : ℕ → ℝ}
    (h0 : ∀ n, 0 ≤ w n) (h1 : ∀ n, w n ≤ 1)
    (hsupp : ∀ n, w n ≠ 0 → (n ^ 2 + 1).Prime) (X : ℕ) :
    ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 X, w n ≤ (primeCount X : ℝ) := by
  exact le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun i hi => show w i ≤ if Nat.Prime ( i ^ 2 + 1 ) then 1 else 0 by specialize hsupp i; aesop ) ( by norm_cast; simp +decide [ primeCount ] )

/-- **Conditional lower bound for primes `n² + 1` (Landau's conjecture, conditional
on the asymptotic-sieve input).**  Given a Friedlander–Iwaniec-type weighted
lower-bound input `hSieve`, the number of `n ≤ X` with `n² + 1` prime is eventually
at least `c · X / (log X)²`.  This is an unconditional *implication* (no GRH)
obtained by dominating the sieve weights by the prime indicator
(`weighted_sum_le_primeCount`); the hypothesis `hSieve` packages the analytic
content that the Friedlander–Iwaniec asymptotic sieve is designed to produce. -/
theorem conditional_landau_lower_bound {c : ℝ} (hc : 0 < c)
    (hSieve : SieveLowerInput c) :
    ∃ c' : ℝ, 0 < c' ∧
      ∀ᶠ X : ℕ in atTop, c' * (X : ℝ) / (Real.log X) ^ 2 ≤ (primeCount X : ℝ) := by
  obtain ⟨w, h0, h1, hsupp, hbound⟩ := hSieve
  refine ⟨c, hc, ?_⟩
  filter_upwards [hbound] with X hX
  exact hX.trans (weighted_sum_le_primeCount h0 h1 hsupp X)

end PrimesNSqPlusOne

# Key analytic ingredients (explanatory note)

**Local densities / singular series.** For the sequence `n²+1`, the sieve and the
circle method both sum over the *local data* `ρ(p)` = number of roots of `x²+1`
mod `p`. The arithmetic law `ρ(p) = 2` if `p ≡ 1 (4)`, `1` if `p = 2`, `0` if
`p ≡ 3 (4)` (the Gaussian splitting law) is proved here (`rootCount_*`,
`local_solvable_iff`). The Euler product of these densities is the constant `C` in
Iwaniec's asymptotic.

**Sieve.** Iwaniec's 1989 semiprime theorem uses a half-dimensional *linear sieve*
whose upper and lower bounds match. Squeezing them gives the asymptotic; the
abstract squeeze step is proved (`isEquivalent_of_tendsto_ratio`). The remainder
term is handled by a *bilinear (circle-method) estimate* that breaks the parity
barrier — this is the input that is cited, not reproved.

**Asymptotic sieve + zero-density.** Friedlander–Iwaniec (1998) for `a²+b⁴`
introduces the *asymptotic sieve for primes*, fed by a bilinear estimate (circle
method) and *zero-density bounds* replacing GRH. Its output is modelled by
`SieveLowerInput`; the elementary conversion of that weighted output to an honest
prime count is proved (`weighted_sum_le_primeCount`,
`conditional_landau_lower_bound`). The `n²+1` prime lower bound itself is Landau's
open conjecture, so it stays conditional.

# Future Directions — Primes of the Form n² + 1

Derived from the Stage 3 analysis and Stage 4 critique of this research cycle.
Each conjecture is bold and falsifiable, with the decisive insight and a "why
now?" justification. Statuses refer to the formal artifacts in
`Cryptography/PrimesNSqPlusOne.lean` and `Cryptography/SqAddOneDivisors.lean`.

## C1. Quantitative divisor-density of the n²+1 sequence

**Conjecture.** For every `X`, the number of *distinct* primes `≡ 1 (mod 4)`
dividing some `n² + 1` with `n ≤ X` grows at least like `c · X / log X`.

The key insight is that the converse `oddPrime_dvd_some_sq_add_one` already gives
a *root* `n < p` for each such prime, so a counting argument over the box
`n ≤ X` should recover a positive proportion of all `1 mod 4` primes up to `X²`.

Why now? We have the exact "which primes occur" characterization
(`oddPrime_dvd_sq_add_one_iff`) formalized; turning the qualitative `Set.Infinite`
result into a density statement is the natural next quantitative step and needs
only counting infrastructure already in Mathlib.

## C2. Parity-refined Landau bases

**Conjecture.** Apart from `n = 1`, every base `n` with `n² + 1` prime is
divisible by `2` but the quotient `n/2` is *not* forced into any single residue
class mod 4 — i.e. `landau_base_even` is the *only* unconditional congruence
obstruction on the base.

The key insight is that `landau_base_even` is proved purely from the evenness of
`n² + 1` for odd `n`; any further base obstruction would have to come from a
prime `≡ 3 (mod 4)` dividing `n² + 1`, which `oddPrime_dvd_sq_add_one_mod_four`
forbids — suggesting no further constraint exists.

Why now? The minimal-obstruction principle is fully formal on the divisor side;
proving the base side has *no* extra constraint is a clean, testable target
(falsifiable by a single counter-pattern in a finite search).

## C3. Iwaniec P₂ lower bound via the formal sieve skeleton

**Conjecture.** The count of `n ≤ X` with `IsSemiprimeValue n`
(`n²+1` a product of ≤ 2 primes) is `≫ X / log X`.

The key insight is that the same congruence filter that excludes `3 mod 4` prime
factors (`three_not_dvd_sq_add_one`) is exactly the local condition feeding
Iwaniec's half-dimensional sieve; formalizing the sieve's *combinatorial*
skeleton (Buchstab/Selmer weights) is separable from the analytic bound.

Why now? `IsSemiprimeValue` is already defined; a Lean development of the
linear/half-dimensional sieve would unlock this and many neighboring results,
and Mathlib's analytic number theory is mature enough to host it.

## C4. Friedlander–Iwaniec strictly enlarges the Landau form

**Conjecture.** The inclusion `{Landau primes} ⊆ {a²+b⁴ primes}`
(`landauPrime_isFIPrime`) is *strict*: there are infinitely many `a²+b⁴` primes
that are **not** of the form `n² + 1`.

The key insight is that fixing `b = 1` collapses `a²+b⁴` to `a²+1`, so any prime
of the form `a² + b⁴` with `b ≥ 2` (e.g. `a²+16`) that is not a perfect-square
shift witnesses strictness; the Friedlander–Iwaniec count `X^{3/4}` dwarfs the
conjectured Landau count `X^{1/2}/log X`.

Why now? The set inclusion is formalized; quantifying the gap between the two
exponents is a concrete, falsifiable density separation.

## C5. Gaussian-integer bridge to cryptographic splitting primes

**Conjecture.** A prime `p` is usable as a "split modulus prime" for
`ℤ[i]`-based key agreement (i.e. `p` splits in `ℤ[i]`) **iff** `p` divides some
`n² + 1`, and this set has natural density `1/2` among all primes.

The key insight is `oddPrime_dvd_sq_add_one_iff`: divisibility of `n²+1` is
*equivalent* to `p ≡ 1 (mod 4)`, which is exactly the Gaussian-splitting
condition — directly tying the number theory to the cryptographic domain of this
catalog.

Why now? The iff is verified here; combining it with Dirichlet density
(`Nat.infinite_setOf_prime_modEq_one` and its quantitative refinements) makes the
`1/2`-density claim a near-term formalization target.
